about.0:
THE PROPHET AND THE OCELOT - In “The Prophet and the Ocelot” (1985-86), the Baroque is contemplated as a contemporary style peculiar to
the modernity allied to Brazilian nature, creating
a space from which one can question the value
of the sign visual and linguistic of the artist’s
own name. It envelops with its sound the figure
of the prophet Oseas his name means salvation
executed by the sculptor Aleijadinho, whose
shadow delineates the squashed shadow of an
Ocelot. The whole thing covered by a kind of veil
with wings of guinea fowl [a key animal in the
rites and ceremonies of Candomblé]. A work that
adopts and not by chance the format of an authentic altarpiece as a sounding board to interpret signs, the traces that guide a tradition. Barja
remains attentive to the possibilities of this place
where the past moves towards a new thought, a
new form; not by sublimation, but by shedding
light to a place and the word kept in it, where European culture, Brazilian nature and African sap
fuse themselves.

Mercedes Replinger González, extract from the book Instalações Barja - 2005 / “Baroque Stages”.

trecho.2: sfeito and transgressive, Barja opted, from the outset, for installation as the medium for his reflection-dialogue. Taking Barja’s works as a starting point, a series of Brazilian and European theoreticians and artists — Evgene Bavcar, Mercedes Replinger, Adolfo Montejo Navas, Roland Campos, Angélica Madeira, Bené Fonteles and Marília Panitz — produced an important body of reflections that accompany this compilation of records that have survived time. It is possible, in this way, to traverse twenty years of history here through the projects and the installations: “Experiência Tumulto (1985)”, “Cubo Cruz Lápide (1985)”, “O Profeta e a Jaguatirica (1985-86)”, “DO AKD-MICO AO POLE-MICO (1986)”, “Mognus Dei (1990)”, “O Sol de Goethe (1999)”, “São João Beuys (1990)”, “Ser ou não Ser, Ao Gullar (1993)”, “Pega Manet/De Onde Vem A Escuridão (1986)”, “TV Anal (1999)”, “Hermógenes (1999)”, “Obranome (2003)” and “Cultura X Natureza = Barbárie (1998/2005)”. Marília Panitz, in her text “To What Matters, an Answer”, proposes an itinerary for reading Barja’s works based on the concept of the equation, so dear to the artist. In the “enigmas of visual equations” of Barja’s commentary-constructions, the author highlights the condensation of meanings whose tool is humour. Appropriating the sharp steel of irony, armed with a laughter of Oswaldian inspiration, the anthropophagous Barja, under a “strong influence of the neo-concrete movement”, composes a set of installations in which he makes reference, in the title of his instal
trecho.3: his work and in his way of approaching art, which results, among other things, in his master’s dissertation. Barja, at a given moment, finds himself before the contingency of hearing, from the movement’s great theorist, the assertion of the “death of art”. His commentary-response is a work/mausoleum, a declaration of disagreement through the establishment of a play of mirrors in which the prophecy turns back upon whoever pronounces it. A constructive play repeated in the fragility of the structure of another work (another mausoleum), his pyramid of cups with coloured liquids, built over a mirror, his Queóps Brasilis. o profeta e a jaguatirica natureza x cultura = barbárie

trecho.5: of a structurally contradictory, plural and polysemic medium (36). Definitively the axiom — all that one has to do with is what one sees (what you see is what you see) — which Stella had enunciated, now turns into something luminous and prophetic: what you see is not only what you see. Baroque Scenographies In the Book of Resemblances, Edmon Jabés asks himself about the path to be followed in order to reach the sources, the origins of writing, of artistic creation. He said: “First one must be named and then it will be necessary to assume, with one’s own name, the fate of each sound, of each sign that perpetuates them” (37). In “O Profeta e a Jaguatirica” (1985-86), the Baroque is contemplated as a contemporary style peculiar to modernity in alliance with Brazilian nature, forging the place from which one may interrogate the value of the sign, visual and linguistic, of the artist’s own name. There, the words that decline the distinct types of representation — realism, hyper-realism, fantastic realism — are exhibited, sliding in disorder along a plank, like those on which merchandise is displayed, enveloping with their sounds the figure of the prophet Hosea, whose name means salvation, executed by the sculptor Aleijadinho, whose shad
trecho.6: In “O Profeta e a Jaguatirica” (1985-86), Barja selects as the first icon of this representation one of the prophets, Hosea, whom Aleijadinho raised in soapstone within the monumental ensemble of the atrium of the sanctuary of Bom Jesus de Matosinhos, in the Minas Gerais town of Congonhas do Campo, known as Os Profetas (1777-1790). An authentic Baroque scenography organized according to a tense equilibrium of contraries, a play of compensations of exceptional force, at once sumptuous and contained, voluptuous and religious. The figure of Hosea is the most important of the minor prophets, so called for the brevity of their texts, is foun
trecho.7: icate in the present soil the place where the ancient was preserved. Since true recollections must not account for the past, how is one to describe the place in which the researcher took possession of it?” (41). Wagner Barja will undoubtedly listen attentively to the place of this discovery of a past, deformed with an almost savage expressionist power, which projects itself as future, precisely in the same space where it took hold of him: in the land to which he belongs. For this reason, the prophet Hosea inscribes his shadow, almost fusing it, with the trace of an animal native to a region whose species is on the brink of extinction: the Jaguatirica, the Leopardus pardalis, an animal that inhabits the tropical forests, the Caatinga, the Cerrados and the Pantanal and that is often confused with the gato do mato or with the gato maracajá. A beautiful undomesticated animal, of nocturnal and solitary habits, capable of adapting even to degraded environments. The whole ensemble of “O Profeta e a Jaguatirica” is wrapped in feathers of galinha d&#x27;Angola, a bird originating in Africa, a key animal in the rites and ceremonies of Candomblé practice (42). Each of these icons — Aleijadinho, the Jaguatirica and the galinha d&#x27;Angola — convert the ensemble of this piece into u
trecho.8: ce of the vanguard. As Angel González says: “a piece by Duchamp produces interpretations, one by Matisse produces sensations. Yet an image by Beuys produces new images, as though Beuys’s images lacked something: they were incomplete. It is not, then, or so it seems to me, a case of pedagogical hypnosis, but of the persuasive exhibition of something imperfect, insufficient, unresolved” (45). Beuys opens up for contemporary art a dramatic space that seems subsequently to demand the obsessive prolongation of new figures, of new works and, also, the construction of certain legendary accounts. o profeta e a jaguatirica
